source_text: De quo quoniam satis actum est, ad illa properemus, quae super naturali malo Manichaeus olim acute, sed, ut probabo, perplexitate quaestionum deceptus obiecit. Breviter tamen prius, quid Augustinus contra Apostoli testimonium retulerit, ventilemus. Ego ergo cum notam istam operam sexuum a Deo auctore corporum institutam, etiam beati Pauli testimonio apertissime dixissem probari, qui invectus in flagitia eorum, quos in virilis quoque sexus concubitum praecipitarat insania, ait: Relicto naturali usu feminae, accensi sunt in desideria sua [n39] ; intuli Apostolo teste, approbari usum feminae naturaliter institutum. Ad hoc ergo iste rescribens: Non dixit, inquit, Apostolus coniugalem usum, sed naturalem, eum volens intellegi qui fit membris ad hoc creatis, ut per ea possit ad generandum sexus uterque misceri; ac per hoc, cum eisdem membris etiam meretrici quisque miscetur, naturalis est usus, nec tamen laudabilis, sed culpabilis. Non ergo isto nomine, id est, usu naturali, coniugalis est laudata commixtio; sed immundiora et sceleratiora flagitia denotata sunt, quam si illicite feminis, sed tamen naturaliter uterentur [n40] . Id est, hic usus feminae quem pronuntiavit Apostolus naturalem, non intellegitur coniugalis, ut bonus licitusque doceatur; sed ideo, inquit, dictus est naturalis, quia diversitatem sexus ad hoc indicat institutam, ut et commixtui pararetur et partui. Queis molitionibus cum iuvaretur nihil, cur tantum immoratus est? Profecto ob hoc solum, ut hi qui eum sequuntur, solutum putent quod viderint fuisse contactum; ceterum quam nihil dixerit, brevis disputatio palam faciet. Nempe Apostolus feminae usum ait naturaliter institutum, nec commendavit alteram commixtionem primitus ordinatam; sed de eo usu disputans, in quo libidinem cunctis noverat viguisse temporibus, naturalem illam vocavit.
pass_a_gloss: About which since enough has been treated, let us hurry to those things which upon natural evil Manichaeus of old acutely, but, as I will prove, deceived by a perplexity of questions, objected. Briefly nevertheless first let us ventilate what Augustine reported against the Apostle's testimony. I therefore when I had said most openly that that known work of the sexes instituted by God the author of bodies is proved even by the testimony of blessed Paul, who, having inveighed against the outrages of those whom insanity had precipitated even into the coupling of the male sex also, says: The natural use of the female having been left, they were kindled in their desires; I brought in, the Apostle being witness, that the use of the female is approved as instituted naturally. To this therefore this man writing back: The Apostle, he says, did not say marital use, but natural, wanting that understood which is done by members created for this, that through them each sex can be mixed for generating; and through this, when anyone is mixed even with a harlot by the same members, the use is natural, nor nevertheless praiseworthy, but culpable. Not therefore by this name, that is, natural use, was marital mingling praised; but the more unclean and more wicked outrages were marked, than if they used females illicitly, but nevertheless naturally. That is, this use of the female which the Apostle pronounced natural is not understood as marital, so that it be taught good and licit; but therefore, he says, it was called natural, because it indicates that the diversity of sex was instituted for this, that it be prepared both for mingling and for birth. By which molitions when he was helped nothing, why did he delay so much? Surely for this alone, that those who follow him may think loosed what they have seen contacted; for the rest how he said nothing, a brief disputation will make plain. The Apostle indeed says the use of the female was instituted naturally, nor did he commend another mingling first ordained; but disputing about that use in which he knew lust had thrived in all times, he called that natural.

pass_b_english: Since enough has been said about this, let us hasten to the arguments Mani once cleverly advanced concerning natural evil—although, as I shall prove, he was deceived by tangled questions. First, however, let us briefly examine what Augustine replied to the apostle’s testimony. I had said that blessed Paul’s testimony proved most clearly that God, the creator of bodies, instituted the familiar activity of the sexes. Denouncing the shameful acts of those whose madness had plunged them even into intercourse with the male sex, Paul says: ‘Abandoning the natural use of the female, they burned in their own desires’ (Romans 1:27). I inferred, with the apostle as witness, that intercourse with the female is shown to have been naturally instituted.

In response this man writes: ‘The apostle did not say “marital use” but “natural use.” He meant that which takes place with organs created so that the two sexes can unite through them for generation. Consequently, when someone unites with a prostitute using the same organs, it is natural use, yet not praiseworthy but blameworthy. This term, “natural use,” therefore did not praise marital union. It identified acts more unclean and criminal than if they had used women unlawfully but nevertheless naturally’ (Augustine, Marriage and Desire 2.20.35). That is: this intercourse with the female which the apostle called natural is not understood as marital, so as to be shown good and lawful. Rather, he says, it is called natural because it indicates that the difference of sex was instituted to prepare both for union and for birth. Since these exertions gained him nothing, why did he spend so long on them? Certainly only so that his followers might think a point answered merely because they saw it touched. A brief argument will show how he said nothing. The apostle says intercourse with the female was naturally instituted; he did not commend some different union originally ordained. Discussing the intercourse in which he knew sexual desire had flourished at every period, he called it natural.

choices.why: Julian's pudenda libido is the appetite accompanying union, not a created substance of sin.
Julian defends marital union (commixtio) as God's work, not the devil's property.
Julian's Manichaean charge: an evil that is a nature, not a will's act.
